# The Enclosure of Night

For most of human history, nightfall meant true darkness. Step outside any village, any town, anywhere on Earth, and the sky overhead blazed with thousands of stars, the Milky Way arching from horizon to horizon like a river of crushed pearl—bright enough that sailors steered by it, farmers marked their seasons by it, and every culture on the planet looked up and peopled the blackness with gods and beasts and ancestors. Darkness covered half the world for half of every day, and everything that lived had evolved inside it. Then, in the span of a few generations—a blink—we flooded it with light.

In 2016, an international team of scientists produced the first comprehensive atlas of artificial night sky brightness, and the picture it revealed was startling: more than 80 percent of humanity now lives beneath light-polluted skies. The Milky Way is invisible to a third of all people alive, including nearly 80 percent of North Americans. By some recent measurements, the glow of the sky itself is brightening by almost ten percent a year. Do the arithmetic and you arrive at a strange conclusion: the majority of human beings today have never seen the galaxy they were born inside. They know it only as a smudge in photographs, or as the backdrop of planetarium shows.

We lost more than scenery. The historian Roger Ekirch, sifting through diaries, letters, court records, and medical texts from the centuries before electrification, noticed something odd: again and again, people referred matter-of-factly to "first sleep" and "second sleep." It turned out that pre-industrial humans did not sleep in one consolidated block. They went to bed a couple of hours after dusk, slept deeply, and then rose around midnight into a quiet interval of wakefulness lasting an hour or two. They prayed. They read by rushlight. They tended the fire, chatted with neighbors, made love, or simply lay still and thought. Then they returned to sleep until dawn. This rhythm appears in accounts from antiquity through the nineteenth century, across cultures and continents. As streetlights and gas lamps spread through the cities, the interval collapsed. We did not merely extend the day; we amputated an entire mode of consciousness.

What was true of us was truer of everything else. Life spent hundreds of millions of years evolving inside darkness, and the creatures of the night are exquisitely tuned to it. Moths navigate by holding the moon at a fixed angle, a trick that turns every porch light into a fatal trap. Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and scramble toward the brightest horizon—once, the moonlit sea; now, frequently, the sodium glow of a beachfront road. Songbirds migrate in darkness, using the stars to hold their bearing, and cities pull them off course into a maze of glass and glare; after a single autumn night in 2020, volunteers collected nearly a thousand dead warblers and sparrows below one lit convention center in Chicago. Many cities now dim their skylines during migration season, a small penance. Studies suggest that a lone streetlight measurably suppresses the nighttime pollination of nearby plants. The food web frays quietly, in the dark, where we do not think to look.

And our own bodies remember. Melatonin, the hormone that orchestrates sleep, is secreted only in darkness, and blue-rich light—the signature of modern LEDs and glowing phone screens—suppresses it directly. Circadian disruption is now implicated in depression, obesity, diabetes, and cancers severe enough that the World Health Organization classifies overnight shift work as a probable human carcinogen. We treat darkness as empty space, a deficiency to be corrected with lumens. Our cells disagree. They keep an ancient clock, and they want the night back.

Astronomers saw this coming before anyone. Observatories have retreated up mountains and into deserts—the Atacama, Mauna Kea—chasing skies that cities surrendered decades ago, and even those redoubts are threatened by creeping suburbs. Dark-sky reserves are designated now the way wildlife sanctuaries are: patches of preserved night ringed by glare. There is a bitter irony here. We build billion-dollar telescopes and hurl probes across the solar system to study the cosmos, while systematically erasing the one direct experience of the cosmos that every human being once owned for free.

Some cultures understood better than we do what darkness holds. To many Aboriginal Australians, a patch of blackness beside the Southern Cross—the Coalsack, a dark nebula—is not an absence but a figure: the Emu in the Sky, a constellation made not of stars but of shadow, whose position in the heavens signaled when emu eggs were ready to gather on Earth. A constellation of darkness. Even the sky's emptiness carried information. We have inherited the map and bleached out half its markings.

It is tempting to file all this under nostalgia, another soft loss on a long list. But the enclosure of night resembles the enclosure of common land: a shared inheritance quietly privatized, converted into advertising glare and perpetual security floodlights, with nobody consulted. The consolation is that this particular wound is reversible in a way few are. Shielded fixtures, warmer bulbs, dimmers, motion sensors, simply switching off office towers at midnight—and the darkness returns immediately. Unlike an acidifying ocean or a warming climate, the night forgives instantly.

So drive past the edge of town some clear, moonless evening. Kill your headlights where it's legal, climb out, and give your eyes half an hour to open. Then look up, past the last halo of the streets, and find Andromeda: light that left its home two and a half million years ago, before our species existed, arriving patient and undiminished on your retina. That light crossed the whole of interstellar space without stopping. The only obstacle it ever faced was the last forty miles of ours.

What should I write about? Something genuinely interesting to me. Let me think about what would make a compelling ~1000 word piece. Options:

1. An essay on something fascinating — like the nature of memory, the history of a strange thing (lighthouses, libraries, deep sea), the philosophy of maps
2. A short story or creative piece
3. A personal-feeling reflection from the perspective of an AI (though that might be too meta)
4. A meditation on something specific and concrete

I think a well-crafted essayistic piece on something I find genuinely interesting would be best. Ideas:

- Lighthouses: their romance, obsolescence, automation
- The deep ocean / abyssal zone
- The Voynich manuscript
- The concept of "liminal spaces"
- The history of silence
- Maps and the edge of the map ("here be dragons")
- The moon's slow retreat from Earth
- The last speakers of dying languages
- The Antikythera mechanism
- Time perception
- The idea of ruins and what they mean

Let me pick something with rich material. I like the idea of writing about lighthouses — there's poetry in them: automation, the last keepers, Fresnel lenses, the way technology made human vigilance obsolete. Or perhaps something about the deep sea — we know less about it than the moon's surface.

Actually, let me consider writing about the slow disappearance of things — or maybe about night itself, how artificial light has erased darkness. That's evocative: the loss of the night sky, light pollution, how most humans no longer see the Milky Way, the biological importance of darkness, the history of artificial light from candles to LEDs.

Or: write about the fact that Earth's rotation is slowing, days getting longer, the Moon drifting away — deep time stuff.

Another option: an essay on boredom, or on waiting rooms, or on the sound of rain.

Let me go with something like "In Praise of Darkness" or the vanishing night — light pollution essay. It has:
- Personal resonance potential
- Scientific facts (Milky Way invisible to 1/3 of humanity, 80% of North Americans)
- Ecological angles (sea turtles, moths, migratory birds, coral spawning timed to moonlight)
- Historical arc (pre-electricity biphasic sleep, "first sleep" and "second sleep" documented by historian Roger Ekirch)
- Astronomical angle (dark sky reserves, astronomers retreating to mountaintops)
- Philosophical close (darkness as commons, what we lose)

That could be beautiful. Alternatively, lighthouses also have a great arc: from wood fires on headlands, to the Eddystone lighthouse saga, Fresnel lenses concentrating light, keepers' lonely journals, then automation in the 20th century, the last keeper in various countries, and now GPS making them almost ornamental — but still kept because sailors distrust relying solely on satellites. The lens as a masterpiece. The keepers who polished brass. The romance vs. reality (keepers driven mad, wrecks still happening).

Both are good. Let me draft the darkness/night essay since it has more emotional and philosophical depth for 1000 words.

Structure:
1. Opening scene: the Milky Way before electricity / a specific image
2. The scale of light pollution: stats
3. History: Ekirch's segmented sleep discovery — pre-industrial humans slept in two shifts, waking in the middle of the night for quiet hours; artificial light compressed this
4. Ecology: moths drawn to flames, baby sea turtles heading toward hotel glow instead of moonlit surf, birds migrating colliding with lit towers, insects declining around streetlights
5. Astronomy: dark sky places, the irony that city dwellers see fewer stars than a rural child centuries ago
6. Philosophical: darkness isn't absence but presence — circadian biology, melatonin; darkness as commons being enclosed like land; the night as the last wilderness accessible... except it's not anymore
7. Close: an invitation — go somewhere dark, wait 30 minutes for eyes to adjust, see Andromeda — light that left its star 2.5 million years ago landing on your retina

Facts to include (verify accuracy):
- Roger Ekirch, historian at Virginia Tech, "At Day's Close" — documented segmented/biphasic sleep in pre-industrial Europe; "first sleep" and "second sleep" (French: premier sommeil); the wakeful interval used for prayer, chores, intimacy, visiting neighbors.
- Light pollution stats: ~80% of North Americans and 60% of Europeans cannot see the Milky Way (2016 study in Science Advances, Falchi et al., "New World Atlas of Artificial Night Sky Brightness"). One-third of humanity cannot see the Milky Way including 80% of Americans. The atlas says more than 80% of world population lives under light-polluted skies.
- Skyglow brightening ~10% per year in some measures (Kyba et al. 2023 found skyglow increasing ~9.6%/yr based on citizen science Globe at Night data).
- Sea turtles: hatchlings instinctively move toward the brightest horizon, historically the moonlit sea; artificial lights disorient them, causing deaths.
- Migrating birds attracted/disoriented by city lights; "Lights Out" programs in Chicago, NYC, Toronto reduce collisions. A Chicago convention center event killed ~1000 birds in one night (October 2020 McCormick Place).
- Melatonin suppression by blue light; circadian disruption linked to health issues; WHO/IARC classified night shift work as probable carcinogen (Group 2A) in 2007/2019.
- Insects: studies show streetlights reduce insect pollination; moth declines near lights.
- Dark sky places: International Dark-Sky Association (now DarkSky International), founded 1988; natural bridges National Monument first International Dark-Sky Park (2007).
- Andromeda galaxy visible to naked eye under dark skies, 2.5 million light-years away — farthest thing most people can see unaided.
- Full moon brightness comparison; the fact that a few generations ago everyone knew constellations.
- Paul Bogard wrote "The End of Night"; also the term "starlight reserve." Christopher Columbus? Not needed.
- The phrase "light trespass."
- LED transition: cities switching to LEDs often increased brightness/blue-rich light.
- The Milky Way in Japanese/Aboriginal traditions — Aboriginal Australians' "Emu in the Sky" dark constellation — nice touch: a constellation made of darkness itself, the Coalsack.

That Emu detail is gorgeous — a constellation defined not by stars but by a dark nebula. Perfect thematic fit: even in the sky, darkness carries meaning.

Word count target: ~1000 words. Let me aim for 950–1050.

Format considerations: This should be flowing prose, essay style, maybe with a title. No headers needed necessarily — or maybe none at all, just elegant paragraphs. Let me write it carefully, with good rhythm, avoiding purple-prose overload but allowing lyricism.

Ending: invitation — drive beyond the glow on a clear moonless night, let your eyes adjust 30 min, look up. Somewhere up there is the light older than our species.
